name: Wasabi Hot Cloud Storage
summary: S3-compatible object storage sold at one flat price per TB, with no egress or request fees.
intro: Wasabi runs its own object storage in 16 regions across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific. Each region has its own endpoint, such as `s3.eu-central-2.wasabisys.com` for Frankfurt, and a bucket lives in the region you create it in. Wasabi describes its API as “100% bit-compatible” with Amazon S3 and IAM, so S3 SDKs, the aws CLI and backup software work after you change the endpoint and keys. There is one storage class: every object is “hot” and readable at once, with no archive tier to restore from. Buckets support versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle expiration and replication, and the service is designed for 11 nines of durability.

The bill has one line that matters: stored data. Pay as you go costs $7.99 per TB-month in North America and EMEA ($0.0078 per GB), with no fees for egress or API requests. The catches are in the minimums. You pay for at least 1 TB every month, even with an empty account. An object deleted or overwritten before it is 90 days old is billed for the remaining days as “Timed Deleted Storage”. Objects are billed as at least 4 KB. Free egress assumes you download no more each month than you store. Reserved Capacity prepays 1, 3 or 5 years for a discount, and Wasabi Fire, an NVMe class for AI and other latency-sensitive work, is sold by quote.
strengths: A predictable bill: no egress or per-request fees, so restores and full reads add no line items
About a third of the S3 Standard list price per TB ($7.99 against $23 in US East)
Every object is readable immediately, with no restore step or retrieval fee as on archive tiers
Object Lock and support in backup tools such as Veeam make it a common off-site backup target
limits: 90-day minimum storage duration on pay as you go: data deleted or overwritten sooner is billed for the rest of the 90 days, so short-lived files can cost more than on S3
At least 1 TB is billed every month, and every object is billed as at least 4 KB
Free egress is a fair-use promise: if you download more each month than you store, your use case doesn’t qualify, which rules out heavy public downloads
A fair-use mechanism caps each account’s concurrent requests and bandwidth according to how much it stores
One hot class only: there is no cheaper archive tier for data you rarely read

snippet.title: Use the aws CLI against a Wasabi region
source: # every Wasabi region has its own endpoint; this one is Frankfurt
# keep every object version for 30 days; nobody can delete it sooner
aws s3 cp pg-2026-10-05.dump.gz s3://acme-backups/postgres/ --endpoint-url "$WASABI" --profile wasabi

notes: Wasabi’s price is for North America and EMEA; the S3 prices are for US East (N. Virginia).
A minimum storage duration means an object deleted or overwritten sooner is still billed for the full period. On Wasabi it applies to all pay-as-you-go storage, not just a cold tier.

sections.title: Where the 90-day minimum bites
sections.intro: Wasabi’s own docs compare it with S3 Standard, which has no minimum: data deleted within about 23 days is cheaper on S3, and data kept longer is cheaper on Wasabi.

items.name: Good fit
items.text: Backups with 30-day or longer retention, video archives, surveillance footage, datasets that are written once and read now and then.

items.name: Poor fit
items.text: CI artifacts, temporary uploads, caches and logs kept for a week. Each deleted object is still billed until it reaches 90 days.

items.name: Hidden churn
items.text: Overwriting a key is an implicit delete. Upload the same 1 MB object every day and up to 90 copies are billed at once.

items.name: Shorter minimum
items.text: Wasabi can switch an account from a 90-day to a 30-day minimum for new uploads; the docs say other pricing models carry different minimums and point you to sales.

story: David Friend and Jeff Flowers had already built five companies together, most recently Carbonite, the online backup service that went public in 2011. Friend thought cloud storage was turning into a commodity, like long-distance calls after MCI undercut AT&T, and wanted it to work like a utility: “My vision for cloud storage is that it will become like electricity. It will be one-size-fits-all.” They worked under the decoy name BlueArchive, then tried about 200 names before picking Wasabi, “because what we are doing is hot”.

Wasabi launched on 3 May 2017 from a single data center in Northern Virginia. It charged $0.0039 per GB-month with no egress fees, offered one class for primary, secondary and archive data, and claimed six times the speed of S3 at a fifth of the price. Immutable buckets were there from day one, because, Friend said, people lose data to “maliciousness, a virus, or a human error”, not to data-center failures.

The flat price kept selling. By September 2022 Wasabi had more than 40,000 customers and 13 regions, and a $250 million round valued it at over $1.1 billion. By January 2026 it stored more than 3 exabytes in 16 regions, and in April 2026 it bought Seagate’s Lyve Cloud business. The list price has roughly doubled since launch, to $7.99 per TB.

choices.choice: One hot class instead of storage tiers
choices.why: Friend wanted storage to be a simple utility. A single class means no retrieval fees, restore delays or lifecycle rules to plan around.
No egress or request fees makes the bill predictable. The price of that is the 90-day minimum and the fair-use egress rule, which keep out short-lived and download-heavy data.
Backup software, gateways and SDKs written for S3 work unchanged, so existing tools could add Wasabi as a target by changing an endpoint.
Friend saw data lost to ransomware, malice and mistakes rather than hardware, so buckets could be locked against deletion for a set time.
